26821:
Moses is the central human figure of the Hebrew Bible: the Levite child rescued from Pharaoh's genocide, raised as an Egyptian prince, exiled as a shepherd in Midian, and called at the burning bush to lead Israel out of slavery. Through him God sends the plagues, brings Israel through the sea, and makes the Sinai covenant. That covenant gives Israel its law, its priesthood and its tabernacle, and it shapes the rest of Scripture.

The narrative does not idealise him. He kills a man and flees. He argues with God about his calling. He loses his temper, breaks the first tablets in anger, and is barred from entering Canaan for striking the rock at Meribah. Yet he is also described as the meekest man on earth, as the one God spoke with face to face, and as a tireless intercessor who offers himself in place of a rebellious people. Deuteronomy closes by saying no prophet like him has arisen since.

The date of the exodus is debated. 1 Kings 6:1 places it 480 years before Solomon's temple, about 1446 BC. Many scholars prefer about 1260 BC under Ramesses II, because of the city name Rameses (Exod 1:11) and the pattern of early Iron Age highland settlement. Others treat the narrative as largely shaped in later centuries. The New Testament presents Jesus as the prophet like Moses and the mediator of a better covenant, and it also honours Moses as faithful in all God's house.
26822: The text says Moses was a Levite born under Pharaoh's decree, adopted by Pharaoh's daughter, and educated in Egypt (the education is stated in Acts 7:22). He fled to Midian after killing an Egyptian, married Zipporah, and was called by God at Horeb. With Aaron he confronted Pharaoh, led Israel out of Egypt and through the sea, received the law at Sinai, built the tabernacle, and led the people forty years in the wilderness. He was 80 when he spoke to Pharaoh (Exod 7:7) and 120 at his death in Moab. He was forbidden to enter Canaan because of Meribah, and God buried him in an unknown grave. The text calls him very meek, says God spoke with him mouth to mouth, and says no later prophet in Israel was like him. Later Scripture credits him with writing laws and records (Exod 24:4; Deut 31:9) and gives his name to Psalm 90.

Maimonides counts the unique status of Moses' prophecy among his Thirteen Principles. The Passover Haggadah famously barely mentions Moses, keeping the focus on God as Israel's redeemer.

Gregory of Nyssa's *Life of Moses* made his ascent of Sinai a model of the soul's endless progress into God. The Eastern Church keeps a feast of the Prophet Moses on 4 September.

The Egyptian form of his name is often taken as a sign of an authentic memory.

26842: Egypt's New Kingdom (c. 1550–1070 BC) used Semitic labourers in building projects, and the Delta site of Pi-Ramesses fits the name Rameses in Exodus 1:11. No Egyptian text names Moses or the exodus, which is unsurprising given how Egyptian royal records were kept. The Merneptah Stele (c. 1208 BC) shows that a people called Israel was already in Canaan by then. The Sinai covenant follows the shape of ancient Near Eastern treaties, with a historical prologue, stipulations, witnesses, and blessings and curses. Deuteronomy in particular resembles Hittite and Assyrian treaty forms, and the resemblance is used on both sides of the dating debate.
26843: The Torah of Moses became the constitution of Israel and the core of Judaism. Prophets appeal to it, Ezra reads it publicly, and later Judaism is organised around it. In the New Testament Moses appears with Elijah at the Transfiguration (Matt 17:3), and Jesus is presented as the prophet like Moses promised in Deuteronomy 18 (Acts 3:22). Moses' law and Jesus' grace and truth are set side by side (John 1:17). The exodus pattern of slavery, deliverance, covenant and journey to the promised land became a template for Christian baptism and salvation, and later for liberation movements such as the African American spirituals' 'Go Down, Moses'. Moses' laws also shaped Western legal thought.

26892:
Aaron, Moses' elder brother, became Israel's first high priest and founder of the hereditary priesthood. God gave him to Moses as a mouthpiece, and he performed signs before Pharaoh and later bore Israel's names on his breastplate when he entered the sanctuary.

His story holds both honour and failure. He supported Moses at Rephidim, was anointed with holy oil, and ran with incense into a plague to stand between the dead and the living. Yet he made the golden calf at the foot of Sinai, joined Miriam in challenging Moses, and shared in the failure at Meribah that kept him out of Canaan. He died on Mount Hor, and his vestments passed to his son Eleazar.

The Aaronic priesthood that began with him stayed central to Israel's worship until the temple fell. The Letter to Hebrews contrasts it with the priesthood of Christ 'after the order of Melchizedek'.
26893: Aaron was a Levite, three years older than Moses and 83 at the confrontation with Pharaoh. He married Elisheba and fathered Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar (Exod 6:23). He served as Moses' spokesman, worked signs, and helped hold up Moses' arms against Amalek. He made the golden calf, was consecrated high priest, and saw two of his sons die. He challenged Moses with Miriam, stopped a plague with incense, and his staff budded. He died on Mount Hor at 123.

26933:
Miriam is the first woman in Scripture called a prophet. She was the elder sister of Moses and Aaron and is remembered as one of the three leaders God 'sent before' Israel (Mic 6:4). Most readers identify her with the unnamed sister who watched over the infant Moses on the Nile and boldly offered Pharaoh's daughter a Hebrew nurse.

After the sea crossing she led the women of Israel in dance and song. Her two-line refrain is often regarded as one of the oldest pieces of poetry in the Bible. Later, with Aaron, she challenged Moses' unique authority, was struck with a skin disease, and was healed through Moses' prayer, and the whole camp waited for her seven days. She died at Kadesh shortly before Aaron and Moses. Deuteronomy cites her affliction as a warning, while Micah ranks her with her brothers as a leader of the exodus.

With Aaron she spoke against Moses, was struck with leprosy (a skin disease), and was shut out of the camp seven days. She died and was buried at Kadesh. Micah names her with Moses and Aaron as sent before Israel, and the genealogies list her as a child of Amram and Jochebed. The sister in Exodus 2 is not named there.
